name: CANOPY SUPER APP
description: Founding Frontend Engineer for Canopy Network — zero-to-one architecture for a Web3 super app that held 25K+ concurrent users at testnet launch.
dossier: I joined Canopy Network as Founding Frontend Engineer and owned the end-to-end frontend for a decentralized L1 that lets teams launch nested chains with their own business logic and tokenomics. I designed and shipped the super app — launchpad, DEX, and chain explorer — as one product rather than three surfaces. The testnet launched with more than 25,000 concurrent users in the first week, and that architecture is still the foundation of the app.

There was no frontend codebase and no senior precedent. Every foundational decision had to be made from scratch against a fixed launch date. I set the stack — React, Next.js, and Node.js — and sequenced delivery around product need: launchpad first so teams could discover and create chains, then the DEX, then the explorer.

I treated blockchain integration, reliability, and SEO as launch constraints, not later work. The frontend stayed stable through testnet traffic at that scale and did not require a rewrite afterward. Most of that original architecture is still in production.

name: TIMOTHY SYKES
description: Lead Full-Stack Engineer for TimothySykes.com — Nuxt on Cloudflare Workers, request-time data, and SEO as infrastructure.
dossier: I owned frontend and web services for TimothySykes.com as Lead Full-Stack Engineer of a four-person team. The site is Tim Sykes' trading-education and publishing platform — news, quote pages, blog, webinars, and lead-capture funnels — on a Nuxt 3 frontend. It shares Songbird with StocksToTrade for quotes, catalogs, WordPress publishing, and OG images rather than running a separate market-data stack.

The brand had to stay loud without paying a rebuild tax on every release. I rebuilt news and quote pages, migrated hosting from Netlify to Cloudflare Workers, and replaced slow full-site builds with request-time data from DynamoDB catalogs, S3 JSON, and a shared cache. Live quotes arrive over Songbird WebSockets. WordPress publishing is automated, so posts go live without a deploy.

I replaced AdButler with AIZEn, including Watch Live and UTM attribution, and shipped SEO as infrastructure: JSON-LD, dynamic sitemaps, robots, redirects, OG images, and correct 404s. Cypress covers core flows, the blog, and ads. Performance work targeted hydration, layout shift, and impression tracking so Core Web Vitals hold when campaign traffic spikes.

name: STOCKS_TO_TRADE
description: Lead Full-Stack Engineer for StocksToTrade — trading education and live market data for 1M+ monthly users.
dossier: I led frontend and web services for StocksToTrade as Lead Full-Stack Engineer of a four-person team. StocksToTrade is a trading education and market-data platform — charting, scanners, watchlists, webinars, and news — used by more than a million unique visitors a month. Songbird, a backend I designed and still own, is the shared service layer for quotes, catalogs, and publishing.

Full-site rebuilds could not keep up with live markets or editorial cadence. I moved the platform to request-time architecture: DynamoDB catalogs, S3 JSON, and a shared cache so pages compose on the request instead of waiting for a rebuild. Live quotes, index feeds, and scanners run over WebSockets, with cache windows and fallback snapshots so watchlists stay current under load.

I automated publishing so WordPress ships news to S3 and the public site SSRs it — editorial no longer blocks deploys. I replaced AdButler with our AIZEn ad stack, led LLM tooling for QA, SEO integrity, and comment moderation, and treated Core Web Vitals as a product feature: JSON-LD, sitemaps, hydration budgets, and cache TTLs. CI/CD and infrastructure on Cloudflare Workers/Pages and AWS cut a large share of operating cost.
tasks: LLM tooling and infra cost cut

name: CONTENT AUTOMATION WITH AWS, JAVASCRIPT, AND WORDPRESS
description: How I automated featured images for a Nuxt + headless WordPress publisher — Lambda, Canvas, and OpenAI instead of a daily CMS chore.
dossier: I was building a Nuxt SSG on headless WordPress for a tech publisher that had already moved article drafting onto AI. The remaining bottleneck was me: every post still needed a featured image, and I was updating them by hand every day.

Image-generation APIs were too slow and too expensive to run on Lambda, so I composed the art instead. ChatGPT wrote the tagline and scored sentiment from the post; a Node canvas job layered branded templates, textures, and blend modes; WordPress REST uploaded the file as media.

Editorial stopped publishing empty-looking posts, and the designer went back to actual brand work. When a specific image missed, the next step was a WordPress plugin so they could regenerate one post without paging me.

name: HOW TO IMPROVE PAGE LOAD TIMES AND WEB CORE VITALS
description: After a Nuxt redesign, I cut post-navigation load time 45% — preconnect, deferred embeds, and REST instead of GraphQL for above-the-fold post data.
dossier: After a two-month Nuxt redesign went live, Lighthouse and Core Web Vitals flagged FCP and Total Blocking Time on post navigation. I traced it to GraphQL on flagship pages, request waterfalls, and iframes that could not defer.

I preconnected fonts and the CMS origin so first-time visitors were not paying connection cost at render. Above-the-fold embeds — a live scanner SPA and an audio player — moved behind a delayed mount so they stopped competing with LCP.
Above-the-fold post data moved from GraphQL to REST, with a slug-to-ID dictionary for SPA navigation. Comments, tags, and related posts stay on GraphQL in onMounted. Initial load dropped about 45%.
tasks: GraphQL to REST for above-the-fold data
